transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Alvarez (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Aurum CTO), Sofia Martinez (Aurum SRE), Daniel Cho (Aurum Lead ML)

Auto summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Demo of Redwood traffic fabric and API keying topologies for multi-tenant routing, quotas, and burst handling.
- Discussed org vs project keys, sticky routing, quota slices, and private/VPC implications (KMS, audit logs).
- Agreed to run benchmarks with Aurum traffic and follow up with pricing/pilot next week.

Topics: traffic fabric, key topology, quota slices, burst policies, private deployment, security/compliance

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Luis, our SE. Um, quick roll call?
[00:08] Evan: Evan here. Sofia and Daniel with me. Appreciate you fitting this in.
[00:12] Luis: Hi all, Luis. We'll jump into a short deck then live demo on the console and the optimize suggestions.
[00:18] Maya: Goal is to walk through traffic fabric — how org and project keys map to routing lanes, how quotas are carved, and how to handle spikes without blowing your egress budget. Also cover security items.
[00:30] Sofia: Quick context: we run a multi-tenant inference service, about 120 tenants, high variance in QPS. Some tenants are latency sensitive (millis), others are batch. We need predictable cost and strong isolation for PII workloads.
[00:45] Daniel: Also want to limit cross-tenant noisy neighbor issues; haven't figured out a good keying model yet.
[00:52] Luis: makes sense. So top-level pattern we recommend is an org key for global billing + project keys for tenant-level routing. You can combine namespaces and project-key slices to do fairshare and burst.
[01:08] Evan: Sorry, "project-key slices" — can you unpack that?
[01:12] Luis: Sure. Think of slices as soft quota lanes. Each project key gets a baseline slice, then you can attach a burst pool at the org level for occasional spikes. The console will show token consumption per slice.
[01:27] Maya: I'll share the console — live. (screen sharing) Opening the traffic fabric view. You can see an example org with two project keys, one pinned to a dedicated pool and the other routing to hosted models.
[01:40] [00:01:40 audio glitch] Speaker 4: -- sorry caught a hiccup --
[01:45] Sofia: Looks like you have sticky routing too? We need some tenants always on dedicated infra for compliance.
[01:49] Luis: Yep. Sticky routing + routing policies: by project key you can pin to capacity tiers (dedicated/dedicated-burst/hosted). For compliance, you'd want dedicated pools + VPC private link.
[02:01] Daniel: How do rollouts/ fallbacks work if a dedicated pool runs out?
[02:05] Luis: We have automatic fallback policies — you can set failover to equivalent model variants in hosted or to a lower-cost quantized variant. There's grace limits so you won't have silent failures; it's all logged.
[02:16] Maya: question for Aurum: what's your current SSO and KMS setup? Are you using a cloud KMS or on-prem HSM?
[02:24] Evan: We're on Okta SAML for SSO and using CloudKMS for encryption keys, but we're evaluating HSM for certain tenants.
[02:31] Maya: good, Redwood integrates with Okta and common KMS providers. HSM or customer-managed keys require private deployment or dedicated VPC with KMS integration.
[02:40] Sofia: What's the audit log granularity? We need per-request headers and user identity mapping for SOC2.
[02:46] Luis: Our audit logs capture request id, project key, model id, latency, token counts, and any policy evaluation results. We can push logs to your SIEM or S3. Retention is configurable.
[02:58] Evan: Are there any nuances around KV cache or prefix caching when you route tenants between pools? We worry about cold starts and cache misses on fallovers.
[03:06] Luis: excellent point. We support KV cache warmers and prefix caching strategies. When a request fails over, the system attempts to warm the KV cache with recent keys for that tenant; but cross-pool cache transfer has limits — you may see a small latency bump on first requests. We recommend pre-warming for planned failovers.
[03:24] Daniel: that "KV" was transcribed as kay-vee in our last call haha.
[03:28] [03:28] Maya: chuckle. transcription artifacts aside — moving on to quotas.
[03:33] Luis: Quota constructs: concurrency quotas (tokens/concurrency per project key), token budgets (monthly), and sliding-window QPS limits. You can set hard and soft limits and configure policy behavior: reject, queue, or degrade (e.g., quantized model).
[03:48] Sophie: (misattributed) We need per-tenant burst allowances; sometimes customers run monthly batch jobs that spike. How do you handle that without letting them exhaust org budgets?
[03:58] Luis: Use a burst bucket at the org level with rate-limited drain and per-project refill rules. You can also set priority lanes so critical tenants borrow from a reserve first.
[04:09] Evan: Any tooling to visualize cost impact if we enable high burst or lower latency?
[04:14] Maya: yes — Optimize module gives per-route recommendations and simulated cost delta when you change batching, quantization, or route a tenant to dedicated. We'll demo that in a minute.
[04:25] [04:25] Speaker 1: brief pause while demo loads
[04:33] Luis: Opening Optimize: here's a workload profile, predicted token throughput, and suggested quantization level for 95th pct. It also shows estimated cost savings and latency trade-offs.
[04:45] Daniel: Can Optimize recommend batching windows that respect low-latency SLAs? We can't increase latency for certain tenants.
[04:51] Luis: yes — constraints can be encoded as per-project SLAs. Optimize will only suggest batching that keeps P95 under your threshold; otherwise it suggests caching or routing to dedicated infra.
[05:05] Sofia: We need stronger guarantees — can we set guaranteed throughput for a tenant?
[05:09] Luis: That's exactly what Dedicated pools are for. You reserve GPU capacity and pin project keys to it, guaranteeing throughput. We also offer autoscale policies for dedicated pools with guardrails.
[05:21] Evan: How does billing work for mixed usage? If a tenant is pinned to dedicated but occasionally routes to hosted fallback, who pays for that?
[05:30] Maya: Billing model: reserved capacity is billed on committed capacity. Fallbacks to hosted incur usage charges on top. We surface per-project cost breakdown so you can charge internal teams.
[05:40] Evan: good. Also want to double-check: data residency requirements — some tenants must stay in EU region. How do you handle region routing?
[05:48] Luis: You can set regional routing rules tied to project keys or org config. If a request from a tenant tagged EU arrives, routing policy keeps it in EU zones. Fallbacks can be region-constrained as well.
[06:00] Daniel: Quick security: If we do private deployment in our VPC, do we still get the console and alerts?
[06:05] Maya: Yes — control plane can be customer-managed; you get the same console and alerting, and logs are shipped to your endpoints. Some enterprise features (like long-retention metrics) are add-ons.
[06:15] Sofia: Are SAML groups mapped to RBAC roles? We want to restrict who can change quota policies.
[06:21] Luis: We integrate SAML -> RBAC mapping, and console actions can be gated behind roles. There's an approval workflow for schema changes if you want multi-person approvals.
[06:30] [06:30] Maya: moving into a short live scenario: assume tenant A (latency critical) and tenant B (batch). We'll show a policy that pins A to dedicated, gives B a small guaranteed baseline and access to org burst.
[06:44] Luis: (typing) creating project keys, setting concurrency 50 for tenant A, baseline 5 rps for tenant B, and org burst = 200 tokens with drain 10/s.
[06:58] [06:58] Daniel: what's the UI callout for sticky routing?
[07:02] Luis: it's a toggle on the key settings "pin to pool"; you can also set sticky session TTL to keep routing consistent for stateful workloads.
[07:13] Evan: And metrics — can we get per-tenant latency histogram in real-time?
[07:18] Luis: Yes, per-project breakdown, P50/P95/P99, token counts, and queue times. We also emit traces if you want to hook to Jaeger.
[07:29] [07:29] Sofia: question on quotas again: is it possible to have a quota that is shared across a group of project keys (e.g., product team uses 10 keys but share a pooled budget)?
[07:37] Luis: absolutely. We call those "quota groups" — you can attach multiple project keys to a shared pool and set group-level budgets and priority arbitration.
[07:46] Daniel: Any gotchas for tenant mapping when you have a thousand keys?
[07:50] Luis: naming and tagging conventions are key; we support namespace hierarchies and dynamic tagging via headers so you can route without proliferating static keys.
[07:59] Maya: quick objection we often hear: "we don't want to manage keys at scale". Redwood: you can auto-generate keys and rotate them, and there's an API for key lifecycle.
[08:09] Evan: About rotation — does rotation cause routing flips or downtime?
[08:13] Luis: rotations are rolling; we allow overlapping validity windows so requests will be smooth.
[08:19] [08:19] Maya: now demoing a trick — conservative fallback: if latency breaches P95, route new requests to a quantized variant while keeping in-flight requests on current path.
[08:31] Daniel: that sounds useful. If we do that do we lose quality for those requests?
[08:35] Luis: slight quality difference; Optimize gives you ROUGE/embedding drift estimates so you can set acceptable deltas.
[08:44] Sofia: legal flagged audit for model changes — do we get model-change alerting when a fallback uses a different checkpoint?
[08:50] Luis: yes, model-change and policy-change events are logged and you can require approval for runtime model swaps.
[08:58] Evan: Let's talk numbers — what's typical latency delta moving from FP16 to 4-bit quant?
[09:03] Luis: depends on model and hardware. On Ampere A100-like, quantization to 4-bit with tuned kernels can improve throughput 1.8x-3x with 10-30% quality cost depending on task. We'll run Aurum traces to give a exact projection.
[09:20] [09:20] Maya: switching to failure scenarios — what happens if our dedicated pool experiences noisy neighbor?
[09:26] Luis: we have guardrails: tenant-level concurrency caps, preemptible burst lanes, and isolate queues per tenant. In extreme cases, we can throttle offending keys and alert you.
[09:41] Daniel: any SLA around failover time?
[09:44] Luis: our platform aims for sub-second routing decisions; practical failover windows are seconds to tens of seconds depending on KV warmup. We expose these metrics.
[09:58] Sofia: Something about the control plane — is it multi-tenant in a private deployment?
[10:03] Maya: In private deployments your control plane can be on your VPC and not shared. In hosted we do multi-tenant control plane but with strong isolation.
[10:13] [10:13] Evan: price question: we're trying to model cost-per-100k requests with a mix of short and long outputs. Do you have a simple calculator?
[10:21] Maya: We do — we'll send a spreadsheet. It includes model-specific tokens, avg tokens per response, batch efficiency, and reserved vs usage pricing.
[10:30] Daniel: I want to flag a constraint: some of our tenants require data never leave EU and logs kept for 7 years. How does Redwood support long-retention logs in private deploy?
[10:39] Luis: if you run private, logs remain in your infra and retention is your policy; for hosted we offer EU-only regions and S3 log exports with retention controls as enterprise add-on.
[10:52] [10:52] Maya: moving to a quick Q&A from the team — 
[10:56] Sofia: can we programmatically reassign quotas during a sale event? We have bursts tied to marketing pushes.
[11:03] Luis: yes, via API you can update allocations dynamically and schedule policy changes ahead of time.
[11:10] Evan: How many keys before performance degrades on routing? We have thousands in one account.
[11:15] Luis: routing table scales horizontally; thousands are fine — main operational concern is organizational clarity and tag hygiene.
[11:24] Daniel: would love an exportable view for billing splits per product team.
[11:28] Maya: console exports chargebacks and per-key cost runs to CSV.
[11:33] [11:33] Speaker 2: brief background noise; quick pause
[11:40] Luis: demoing logs -> here's an example request line: project_key=proj_abc, model=gptx-14k, tokens_in=24, tokens_out=420, latency=180ms. You can make alerts on any of these fields.
[11:55] Sofia: For SOC2, do you provide SOC2 docs and penetration test reports?
[12:00] Maya: yes — SOC2 Type 2 is available; we'll include current certs in the security pack. Pen test summary too.
[12:09] Evan: about SSO — we need to map Okta groups to roles and limit who can change quota policies. Is that supported?
[12:16] Luis: supported. You can also lock certain actions behind approvals.
[12:22] Daniel: Let's discuss the pilot scope: we'd like to run 2 models, one quantized and one FP16, on a slice of traffic for 2 weeks and measure cost and quality.
[12:33] Maya: sounds reasonable. Typical pilot: 2-week pilot, sample traffic replay, a small dedicated pool or reserved capacity, and weekly check-ins.
[12:42] Evan: what do you need from us to kick off?
[12:45] Maya: sample traffic traces, list of tenants and compliance constraints, and expected SLOs. Also decision point on private vs hosted for the pilot.
[12:54] [12:54] Luis: I'll note we can simulate your spike patterns in the sandbox to show expected burst consumption and cost.
[13:02] Sofia: would also like to see a runbook for emergency throttling — if a tenant goes rogue, how quickly can we cut them off?
[13:09] Luis: there are immediate kill switches in the console and API; you can set automatic throttles that trigger on anomalous behaviors.
[13:20] [13:20] Maya: time check — we have 40 minutes left; want to deep dive into the Optimize output?
[13:26] Evan: yes please.
[13:28] Luis: Opening an example Optimize sim: baseline traffic, suggestions: increase batch size to 8 for non-latency tenants, enable prefix caching for repeated prompts, quantize small models to int4. It shows expected cost delta -28% and latency +12ms for the non-critical lane.
[13:48] Daniel: can we pin suggestions to only show for certain keys?
[13:52] Luis: yes, suggestion scope can be per-project-key or org-wide.
[13:56] Sofia: when Optimize suggests caching, what's the TTL? Some of our data changes rapidly.
[14:01] Luis: TTLs are configurable per-route; you can set short TTLs for volatile content and longer for stable responses.
[14:09] [14:09] Evan: switching to procurement question: for Dedicated pools we assume minimum 3-month commitment?
[14:15] Maya: standard committed terms vary; we typically do 1/3/12 month plans depending on customer. We'll include options in the pricing.
[14:25] Evan: do you offer test credits?
[14:27] Maya: yes, pilot credits for first 2 weeks.
[14:30] [14:30] Luis: demoing traffic policy editor — you can write simple JSON policies or use UI templates. There are templates for "latency-critical", "batch", "iso-sensitive".
[14:44] Daniel: is there a way to preview policy impact before applying?
[14:48] Luis: preview mode runs a dry-run against stored traces and shows expected affected requests and cost delta.
[14:57] Evan: any gotcha on header-based routing? We plan to add a tenant-id header; will that be sufficient?
[15:03] Luis: header-based routing works but ensure header authenticity; we recommend signing headers or using mTLS between services.
[15:12] Sofia: we have mTLS internally so that's fine.
[15:16] [15:16] Maya: quick note on observability: token-level tracing can be voluminous; we recommend sampling or aggregated metrics for long-term retention.
[15:28] Daniel: good point.
[15:31] [15:31] Luis: tailoring to Aurum: we'd recommend starting with project keys per product line, a shared quota group for non-critical tenants, dedicated pool for top 5 latency-critical tenants, and an org-level burst bucket for marketing spikes.
[15:50] Evan: sounds aligned. Any examples of customers with similar size?
[15:54] Maya: we have customers in fintech and retail with 100s of tenants; happy to share case study links.
[15:59] [15:59] Sofia: can you show alarm thresholds we should set?
[16:04] Luis: set alerts for token burn rate > expected, P95 latency > SLA, and KV cache miss rate spike. We can provide recommended thresholds based on your baseline.
[16:18] Evan: about failover logging — can we tag fallovers as incidents and auto-page?
[16:24] Luis: yes, integrate with PagerDuty/Slack and tag incidents with project_key and policy_id.
[16:33] [16:33] Daniel: I'd like to see the sample bench results next week.
[16:36] Luis: noted. We'll run bench with both int4 and FP16 and share numbers and the raw traces.
[16:42] Maya: summary time — main decisions: Aurum will share traffic traces and tenant list; Redwood will run bench and share pricing, security docs, and a pilot plan.
[16:53] Evan: timeline: we'll aim to have traces ready by 2027-04-14 and decide pilot mode by 2027-04-18.
[17:00] Maya: perfect. Any final Qs?
[17:03] Sofia: one last: how do you handle GDPR DSARs for logs?
[17:08] Luis: logs can be redacted or exported and we support data deletion flows for private deploy. For hosted, we provide tooling and attestation for DSAR workflows.
[17:18] Daniel: thanks.
[17:20] [17:20] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the pack.
[17:24] Evan: thanks.
[17:25] [17:25] End of recording
